newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Sharif says tackling economy priority.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Sharif says tackling economy priority.

text.p: Pakistan's Nawaz Sharif, saying he expected to win a comfortable majority in national elections, said on Sunday tackling a dire economy would be his first priority as prime minister.
He told Reuters in an interview that repairing the economy would be a long and difficult task, but that he was confident Pakistan could become an "Asian Tiger".
"The economy is in very bad shape because of the mismanagement of the Benazir Bhutto government," said the former prime minister.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
"The banks today are almost bankrupt. Foreign exchange reserves are at an all-time low," he said. "Fixing the economy will be an uphill task, but it is a challenge we must accept."
Sharif, who said he would be content to win around 100 seats in the 217-member National Assembly in Monday's vote, gave few details of how he planned to tackle Pakistan's economic woes.

"We will have to go in for this from all directions," he said. However, he told reporters later his government would offer incentives to foreign investors, reform the tax system and seek to expand the country's industrial base.
Sharif, a Lahore-based industrialist who lost power in 1993, said his previous government had put Pakistan in a position to take off economically.

"Pakistan would have been an Asian Tiger if the momentum had been kept up, but in the last three years things have become very bad," he said. "Unfortunately it will take some time before we can once again become an Asian Tiger."

Sharif's previous government was dismissed on corruption charges but restored by the Supreme Court, only to lose power again two months later. His Pakistan Muslim League lost the October 1993 polls to Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
Last week, the Supreme Court upheld Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto, saying there was enough evidence of corruption, nepotism and other abuses for him to have fired her.
Corruption has been the main issue in a campaign marked more by apathy than the usual passion and Sharif said he would strengthen an anti-corruption commission to root out graft.

"This Accountability Commission is an independent body. We will try to make it free of any government influence so that any citizen can go to it with a petition and the commissioner is free to take action", he said.
He said a Sharif government would not target Bhutto or her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who has been widely accused of corruption. Bhutto and Zardari deny any wrongdoing.
"We will never indulge in any politics of revenge," Sharif declared.
But speaking to a small group of reporters later, Sharif blamed Zardari for many of Pakistan's current problems.
"Zardari was running the country, including the financial institutions. He was effectively de facto prime minister," he said.
Sharif ended his election campaign in Lahore early on Sunday after a parade through the old city that looked like a victory march, with thousands of people packing muddy lanes despite steady rain.
Men let off fireworks in the streets while women threw rose petals from balconies and Sharif said his election campaign had peaked at the right time.
The poor initial response was mostly due to uncertainty over whether the Supreme Court would uphold the dismissal of Bhutto and allow elections to go ahead, he added.
